question: A 63-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his wife because she is concerned he is having another stroke. The patient says he woke up with right-sided facial weakness and drooping. Past medical history is significant for a recent case of shingles treated with acyclovir, and a stroke, diagnosed 10 years ago, from which he recovered with no residual functional deficits. On physical examination, there is weakness and drooping of the entire right side of the face. Sensation is intact. The remainder of the physical examination is unremarkable. Which of the following additional findings would also most likely be seen in this patient?

options.opc: Complete loss of taste to the tongue

paths: (Facial nerve structure)-PART_OF->(Bone structure of cranium)-LOCATION_OF->(Neurologic Examination)-DIAGNOSES->(Aphasia, Expressive)

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Recent case of shingles treated with acyclovir -> possible facial nerve involvement -> right-sided facial weakness and drooping -> 70% CHAIN: Stroke diagnosed 10 years ago with recovery and no residual deficits -> possible recurrent stroke -> right-sided facial weakness and drooping -> 60% CHAIN: Right-sided facial weakness and drooping -> possible involvement of the facial nerve -> possible decreased salivation -> 50% CHAIN: Right-sided facial weakness and drooping -> possible involvement of the facial nerve -> possible wrinkled forehead due to loss of muscle tone -> 40% CHAIN: Right-sided facial weakness and drooping -> possible involvement of the facial nerve -> possible expressive aphasia due to cortical involvement -> 70%
enhanced_information: In a patient with right-sided facial weakness and drooping, additional findings most likely to be seen include decreased salivation and possibly a wrinkled forehead due to loss of muscle tone. Expressive aphasia is less likely to be associated in this context.
analysis: The patient's symptoms are consistent with Bell's palsy, which is a peripheral facial nerve (cranial nerve VII) palsy. This condition typically results in weakness of the entire side of the face, including the forehead, due to lower motor neuron involvement. Bell's palsy can also affect other functions of the facial nerve, such as taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, salivation, and hearing. However, complete loss of taste is unlikely as it would require additional cranial nerve involvement. Decreased salivation is a more common finding due to the involvement of the facial nerve, which innervates the submandibular and sublingual glands. Partial hearing loss can occur due to hyperacusis, as the stapedius muscle, which dampens sound, is innervated by the facial nerve. Expressive aphasia and a wrinkled forehead are not associated with Bell's palsy. Therefore, partial hearing loss is the most likely additional finding.
